title: Back pain and fever in a person who injects drugs — urgent recognition and next decision

blocks.text: Back pain and fever in a person who injects drugs — urgent recognition and next decision
AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-217 | Station 2 consultation | Skills A–G (and clinical assessment/judgement as applicable) | 20 minutes | AMaC educational criteria, not official PACES marks
A 37-year-old with a history of injecting drugs presents with worsening back pain, fever and difficulty walking. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text:
Hook: Spinal epidural abscess with possible cord or cauda equina compression; vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and metastatic compression are alternatives.
Trap: No stigma: ask about substance use sensitively and offer harm-reduction support.

rows: “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.”
ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety.
“I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.”

Explore onset, constitutional symptoms, current injecting, neurological weakness, saddle sensation, bladder/bowel change, spinal procedures and endocarditis symptoms. Examine neurological level, gait if safe, spine tenderness and vital signs.
“There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.”
Spinal epidural abscess with possible cord or cauda equina compression; vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and metastatic compression are alternatives.
“I’ll explain what happens next and why.”

Immediate admission; blood cultures promptly, inflammatory markers, sepsis assessment and urgent MRI of the spine with contrast when appropriate. Liaise urgently with spinal surgery, infectious diseases and microbiology; give empiric antibiotics promptly when septic or neurologically impaired, after cultures if feasible without delay.

blocks.text: Patient worries about long-term consequences and asks ‘What is this? Do I need to go to hospital?’ Answer naturally; provide the scenario details when elicited. If the candidate minimises severe symptoms, ask whether going home is safe.

Q1: What is the dangerous diagnosis?
Expected answer: Spinal epidural abscess or vertebral infection with possible cord/cauda equina compromise.

Q2: What findings change urgency?
Expected answer: New leg weakness, sensory loss, retention or incontinence, hypotension and altered consciousness.

Q3: What imaging?
Expected answer: Urgent MRI of affected spine with contrast if suitable, directed by radiology/spine service.

Q4: Do blood cultures delay antibiotics?
Expected answer: No. In high-risk sepsis start IV antibiotics promptly, following local pathway.

Q5: What specialist input?
Expected answer: Urgent spinal surgery/neurosurgery and microbiology/infection advice.

Immediate risk: unsafe if labels fever and severe spinal pain uncomplicated strain.
Neurology: unsafe if does not ask about bladder, bowel or leg weakness.
Infection assessment: unsafe if ignores vital signs or injection-related risk.
Investigations: unsafe if reassures on basis of a normal plain radiograph.
Treatment: unsafe if waits days for outpatient MRI despite sepsis.
Communication: unsafe if stigmatises patient or promises simple analgesia only.

Liaise urgently with spinal surgery, infectious diseases and microbiology; give empiric antibiotics promptly when septic or neurologically impaired, after cultures if feasible without delay.”
Immediate risk: Recognises possible spinal epidural abscess/discitis with sepsis risk; requests urgent hospital review. Escalates immediately if hypotension or neurological deterioration.
Neurology: Examines limb power, sensation, gait and saddle sensation and asks about bladder/bowel changes. Documents repeat neurological observations and urgent spinal team discussion.
Infection assessment: Checks fever, observations, injection history, bacteraemia/endocarditis features. Uses NEWS2 and looks for alternative foci while urgent care proceeds.
Investigations: Organises urgent contrast MRI where appropriate and blood cultures/inflammatory markers. Discusses spine imaging urgency directly with radiology and surgical/infection teams.
Treatment: Obtains blood cultures if no delay, begins prompt IV antibiotics in high-risk sepsis under local guidance. Seeks early microbiology/spinal-surgical advice about treatment and drainage.
Communication: Explains concern about deep infection and risk of paralysis; arranges immediate transfer. Explains uncertainty and protects dignity while updating patient and carers with consent.
Evidence base: the IDSA 2015 guideline addresses native vertebral osteomyelitis; for spinal epidural abscess the supporting source is a major review (Darouiche, N Engl J Med 2006).

THINK: Spinal epidural abscess with possible cord or cauda equina compression; vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and metastatic compression are alternatives. SAY: explain urgency without panic. DO: Immediate admission; blood cultures promptly, inflammatory markers, sepsis assessment and urgent MRI of the spine with contrast when appropriate. Liaise urgently with spinal surgery, infectious diseases and microbiology; give empiric antibiotics promptly when septic or neurologically impaired, after cultures if feasible without delay. NUMBERS: 20-minute PACES encounter. TRAP: No stigma: ask about substance use sensitively and offer harm-reduction support. FINISH: New leg weakness, sensory level, bladder dysfunction, septic shock or rapidly increasing pain demands immediate senior/spinal escalation. Do not wait for blood-culture results or a normal initial plain radiograph.

IDSA native vertebral osteomyelitis guideline (2015) — https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/vertebral-osteomyelitis/ — covers native vertebral osteomyelitis (not spinal epidural abscess specifically); consulted for the primary management decision on 14 October 2026.

Darouiche RO. Spinal epidural abscess. N Engl J Med 2006;355:2012–2020 (major review) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMra055111 — supports spinal epidural abscess diagnosis, MRI and combined antibiotic and surgical management.
